period: Old Kingdom, Fourth Dynasty, c. 2600-2500 BC
summary: Three kings, three generations, one century: Giza is a planned city of the dead, and the pyramids are only its tallest buildings.
look: You are on a limestone shelf at the edge of the Western Desert, about 9 km west of the Nile, with Cairo pressing right up to the foot of the slope. The three big pyramids march diagonally from north-east to south-west: Khufu's, Khafre's (the one with a pale cap of casing near the top) and the much smaller Menkaure's. The Sphinx crouches at the bottom of the slope to the east, beside Khafre's valley temple, and fields of flat-topped tombs spread east and west of the Great Pyramid.
story:
Giza was built in roughly a century by one family. Khufu went first and chose the highest, firmest rock. His son Khafre built beside him on slightly higher ground, and Khafre's son Menkaure built a smaller third. The Greek names you will hear, Cheops, Chephren and Mykerinos, come from Greek writers such as Herodotus, who visited around 450 BC and was told tall stories by local guides, just as you may be today.

Each pyramid was only the centre of a machine for eternity. On its east face stood a mortuary temple where priests brought offerings every day. A covered causeway ran down to a valley temple at the edge of the floodplain, where canals and a harbour received boats. Around the king were small pyramids for queens, pits for boats, and streets of mastabas, the bench-shaped tombs of relatives and officials, laid out on a grid like a town. Priests kept some of these cults running for centuries.

What the pyramids did not need was slaves. South-east of the Sphinx, beyond a great stone wall, archaeologists have found the bakeries, breweries and barracks of the workforce, and a cemetery where workmen and foremen were buried near the monuments they built.

Today the plateau is the northern end of the UNESCO site 'Memphis and its Necropolis', and a recent revamp has been adding a visitor centre, electric buses and a restaurant at the panorama point. The general ticket covers the open-air site; the interiors of the pyramids and tombs such as Meresankh's need separate tickets and open on rotation, so check at the ticket office.
details: Top of Khafre's pyramid: the surviving cap of smooth casing shows how all three pyramids once looked.
Great Pyramid, north face: the original entrance high up under stone gables, and the robbers' tunnel visitors use below it.
West of the Great Pyramid: walk down a 'street' between the mastabas of Khufu's officials.
South-west of Menkaure's pyramid: the panorama point, for the classic photo of the whole group.
Camels and horses: agree the total price, route and return before you mount; a smiling 'la shukran' is enough to decline.
fun_fact: Herodotus was told that an inscription on the Great Pyramid recorded the money spent on radishes, onions and garlic for the workers. He took it seriously; your guide may offer similar gems.
narration: You are standing on the Giza plateau, a shelf of desert limestone above the Nile valley, and everything you can see was planned by one family in about a century, some 4,500 years ago. Khufu came first and built the biggest pyramid. His son Khafre built the second, on slightly higher ground, and Khafre's son Menkaure built the third, much smaller. The Greeks called them Cheops, Chephren and Mykerinos, and Herodotus came here as a tourist around 450 BC. Think of each pyramid as the tallest building in a complex. On its east side stood a temple for daily offerings. A covered causeway ran down to a valley temple at the edge of the old floodplain, where boats arrived. Around the king lay small pyramids for his queens, pits for full size boats, and whole streets of flat tombs called mastabas, the Arabic word for bench, for his relatives and officials. The Sphinx crouches at the bottom of the slope beside Khafre's valley temple. A good order is the Great Pyramid first, then the panorama point, Menkaure and Khafre, and the Sphinx last, on your way out. When the camel and horse men approach, agree the full price and the route before you climb on, or smile, say la shukran, and keep walking. Now look at the top of the second pyramid: that pale cap is original casing, and once all three shone like that.

period: Old Kingdom, Fourth Dynasty, reign of Khufu, c. 2600-2560 BC
summary: The only Ancient Wonder still standing: 2.3 million blocks, set so precisely that its sides face true north within a fraction of a degree.
look: You are facing the largest pyramid ever built in Egypt: each side about 230 m long, about 138.5 m high today after losing its top 8 m. Stand at the north face. High up, left of centre, is the original entrance under a double row of huge stone gables; lower down and slightly to the right is the forced tunnel that visitors use. The stepped surface is the backing masonry: the smooth white casing has gone, except for a few blocks at the foot of this face.
story:
Khufu's builders called it Akhet Khufu, 'Horizon of Khufu'. It took roughly 26 years and was probably directed by his nephew Hemiunu. Its original height was 146.6 m, 280 royal cubits, and for more than 3,700 years nothing built by humans was taller, until the spires of medieval English cathedrals overtook it.

The numbers are absurd. About 2.3 million blocks weighing some 6 million tonnes, most of them limestone cut from a quarry just south of here, with granite for the burial chamber shipped more than 900 km from Aswan. Yet the base is level to within about 2 cm, the four sides match in length to within a few centimetres, and they face true north within about a fifteenth of a degree. Nobody knows exactly how they did it: the sun, the stars and plumb lines all have their champions.

It was once sheathed in polished white limestone from Tura, across the river. Earthquakes loosened the casing and medieval Cairo used the pyramid as a quarry; in 1356 Sultan Hassan, whose great mosque you will see on the 16th, had casing stones carted into the city.

The tourist entrance is a robbers' tunnel. Tradition credits the caliph al-Ma'mun, around 820 AD, but many scholars think robbers dug it much earlier. And the pyramid still has secrets: in 2017 muon detectors revealed a 'Big Void' at least 30 m long above the Grand Gallery, and in 2023 a camera looked into a 9 m corridor hidden behind the entrance gables.
details: North face, high and left of centre: the original entrance, about 17 m up, under its double row of gable stones.
Around that entrance: a hieroglyphic text carved in 1842 by Lepsius's Prussian expedition in honour of their king.
Foot of the north face, near the middle: surviving Tura casing blocks, smooth and angled. Imagine the whole pyramid like that.
Look closely at the core blocks: many are full of coin-shaped fossil shells from the sea that once covered Egypt.
South side: the two pits where Khufu's dismantled cedar boats lay sealed for 4,500 years.
fun_fact: Herodotus was told the pyramid took 100,000 men, in three-month shifts, 20 years. Pliny tells how the Greek sage Thales measured its height from its shadow.
narration: This is the Great Pyramid of Khufu, the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and the only one still standing. It was finished about 4,500 years ago, after some 26 years of work, and its builders called it Akhet Khufu, the Horizon of Khufu. It rose 146 metres, and for more than 3,700 years nothing built by human hands was taller. Today it is about 8 metres shorter, because the tip and the smooth white casing have gone. Medieval Cairo used the pyramids as a quarry, and in 1356 Sultan Hassan had casing stones carted into the city. What you see now is the stepped core: about 2.3 million blocks, mostly quarried right here on the plateau, with granite for the burial chamber shipped more than 900 kilometres from Aswan. The precision is the real shock. The base is level to within about 2 centimetres, and the sides face true north within a fraction of a degree. The tourist entrance below the original one is a robbers' tunnel, traditionally blamed on the caliph al-Mamun around 820 AD. And the pyramid is still giving up secrets: in 2017, particles from space called muons revealed a large hidden void above the Grand Gallery, and in 2023 a camera peered into a sealed corridor behind the entrance. Now look high on the north face, left of centre, for the original doorway under its giant stone gables.

period: Old Kingdom, Fourth Dynasty, reign of Khufu, c. 2600-2560 BC
summary: A stooping climb through a robbers' tunnel to the 8.6 m high Grand Gallery and a granite chamber with a sarcophagus too wide for the passage.
look: The route runs through the robbers' tunnel, up the low Ascending Passage (about 1.2 m high, so you stoop for nearly 40 m), into the soaring Grand Gallery, through a cramped antechamber and into the King's Chamber. That chamber is a granite box about 10.5 by 5.2 m and 5.8 m high, with the lidless sarcophagus near the west wall. It is hot, humid and steep, with wooden boards and handrails; photo rules change, so check at the entrance.
story:
Nothing inside is painted or inscribed: the drama is pure architecture. After the burial, three granite plugs were slid down the Ascending Passage to seal it. The robbers' tunnel simply loops around them through softer limestone, which is why you join the passage just above the plugs.

Then the roof lifts away. The Grand Gallery is 46.7 m long and 8.6 m high, its walls stepping inwards in seven courses of corbelling until the gap at the top is just 1 m wide. A central ramp runs between two benches cut with 28 slots on each side. Nobody is sure what they held: beams to restrain the granite plugs, perhaps, or part of a hauling system.

The King's Chamber is lined with red Aswan granite. Its flat ceiling is nine slabs weighing about 400 tonnes in total, all cracked because the chamber settled a few centimetres. The sarcophagus, cut from a single block with copper saws and tube drills, is wider than the passage you came up, so it was placed here before the roof went on. Above you are five low 'relieving chambers'. Nathaniel Davison found the first in 1763; in 1837 Colonel Howard Vyse blasted into the other four with gunpowder and found red-painted names of work gangs, such as 'Khufu excites love', the graffiti that tie this pyramid to Khufu.

The Queen's Chamber below, often closed, has two narrow shafts. In 1993 Rudolf Gantenbrink's robot crawled 65 m up the southern one and found a small stone 'door' with two copper pins; later cameras found red-painted marks behind it. The muon-detected 'Big Void' lies somewhere above the Grand Gallery, unreached.
details: Where you join the Ascending Passage: the end of a granite plug, bypassed by the robbers' tunnel.
Grand Gallery walls: count the seven corbelled steps closing in overhead.
Grand Gallery floor: the rows of rectangular slots along both side benches.
Antechamber: vertical grooves in the granite where portcullis slabs once dropped.
King's Chamber, north and south walls about 90 cm above the floor: the openings of the two narrow shafts.
fun_fact: A cedar plank Waynman Dixon pulled from a Queen's Chamber shaft in 1872 went missing in Aberdeen and turned up in a cigar tin in 2020. It dates to centuries before Khufu.
narration: You are about to climb into the heart of the Great Pyramid, and nothing inside is painted or inscribed: the drama is pure stone. You enter through a robbers' tunnel, then join the original Ascending Passage just above three granite plugs that sealed it after the burial. The passage is barely 1.2 metres high, so stoop and take your time. Then the ceiling suddenly lifts away. This is the Grand Gallery, 8.6 metres high and almost 47 metres long, its walls stepping inwards in seven courses until the gap at the top is only 1 metre wide. Nobody knows exactly what the slots along its floor were for. Through a low antechamber, where granite portcullis slabs once dropped, you reach the King's Chamber, a box of red Aswan granite. Its ceiling is nine slabs weighing about 400 tonnes, all cracked. The sarcophagus is wider than the passage you came up, so it was placed here while the pyramid was still being built. Above your head are five low relieving chambers. In 1837 Colonel Howard Vyse blasted his way into them with gunpowder and found the builders' graffiti, painted gang names like Khufu excites love, and that is how we know this was Khufu's pyramid. Before you leave, find the small rectangular openings in the north and south walls: shafts that run all the way to the outside.

period: Old Kingdom, Fourth Dynasty, reign of Khufu and after, c. 2580-2500 BC
summary: Three small pyramids for the women of Khufu's family and a planned cemetery for his children, on the sunrise side of the Great Pyramid.
look: On the east side of the Great Pyramid stand three small pyramids in a north-south line, each about 45-49 m along the base, now ragged and stepped: G1a in the north, then G1b, then G1c in the south. East of them stretch rows of big double mastabas for Khufu's children, with Meresankh III's tomb on the far side.
story:
Queens' pyramids normally stood south of the king's, but Khufu's quarry was there, so his went east. Mark Lehner argued that the northern one, G1a, belonged to Hetepheres I, Khufu's mother; G1b is usually given to Queen Meritites I and G1c to Henutsen. Excavations in 1991-1993 found the base and capstone of a fourth, tiny 'cult' pyramid, G1d, near the Great Pyramid's south-east corner.

In 1925, the story goes, a photographer of George Reisner's Harvard-Boston expedition set up his tripod near G1a and one leg sank into plaster. Below lay shaft G7000X with Hetepheres I's gilded furniture and her alabaster sarcophagus, sealed and empty. Her body has never been found.

East of the queens, Khufu laid out twelve double mastabas in rows for his children: Kawab, the eldest son, with his wife Hetepheres II; Khufukhaf; Hordjedef, remembered later as a sage. The great mastaba G7510 belonged to Ankhhaf, Khufu's half-brother and vizier, the boss named in the Diary of Merer. More than a thousand years later, a temple of 'Isis, Mistress of the Pyramids' grew up against G1c; it was rebuilt in the 21st Dynasty.
details: Northernmost small pyramid, G1a: probably built for Khufu's mother, Hetepheres I.
Near the Great Pyramid's south-east corner: the low base of the tiny cult pyramid G1d, found only in the 1990s.
North-east of G1a: the shaft G7000X, where Hetepheres I's furniture was found in 1925 (now in Cairo).
Against the east face of G1c: remains of the later temple of Isis, Mistress of the Pyramids.
East of the queens: the rows of double mastabas of Khufu's children, with Ankhhaf's huge G7510 beyond.
fun_fact: Hetepheres I's sarcophagus was sealed but empty, yet her canopic chest still held her embalmed organs, among the oldest evidence of royal embalming.
narration: These three small pyramids in a row, on the sunrise side of the Great Pyramid, belonged to the women of Khufu's family. Queens were normally buried south of the king, but Khufu's quarry was there, so his queens went east. The northern one probably belonged to his mother, Hetepheres. The other two are usually given to Queen Meritites and to Henutsen. In 1925, the story goes, a photographer's tripod sank into a patch of plaster nearby. Underneath was a deep shaft holding Hetepheres' gilded furniture and her alabaster sarcophagus, sealed and empty. Her body has never been found. Further east, Khufu laid out his children's tombs in neat rows, like houses on a street: his eldest son Kawab, Khufukhaf, Hordjedef. The biggest belonged to Ankhhaf, his half brother and vizier, the boss of the boatman Merer whose diary changed what we know about the pyramid. Now look at the southern little pyramid: against its east face are the remains of a temple to Isis, Mistress of the Pyramids, which grew up here more than a thousand years later.

period: Old Kingdom, late Fourth Dynasty, c. 2520 BC
summary: A queen's tomb that still has its colours: Khufu's granddaughter, carved in the rock with a row of ten women of her family.
look: Steps lead down from the Eastern Cemetery, about 2 m below street level, into a rock-cut chapel beneath a mastaba. Inside are three rooms with painted reliefs and pillars; on the north side, a row of ten standing female figures is cut from the living rock. Lighting is low, so give your eyes a minute.
story:
Meresankh III had royal blood on every side. Her mother, Hetepheres II, was a daughter of Khufu; her father was Prince Kawab, Khufu's eldest son; and she married King Khafre. She died at about 50 to 55, a small woman of 1.54 m.

Her mother most likely commissioned this tomb for her, and an inscription records that Hetepheres II gave her daughter the black granite sarcophagus, carved like a palace facade. Another inscription by a doorway says Meresankh was buried 272 days after her death, a long delay that may mean her death was unexpected. George Reisner's Harvard-Boston team found the tomb in 1927, on what was meant to be the last day of the season. Robbers had long ago propped the sarcophagus lid open with stones and thrown her skeleton into a corner. The tomb also held what are often called the earliest known canopic jars, and a statue of Hetepheres II embracing her daughter, now in Boston.

The walls show her family and her estate: bread baking, beer brewing, fowling, herding, metalworking and sculptors carving her statues. The row of ten women is usually read as Meresankh with her mother and daughters, an all-female family portrait.
details: North wall of the first room: Hetepheres II on the left and Meresankh III on the right.
North side of the tomb: the row of ten female figures cut from the rock.
West wall: the false door, with sculpted figures beside it.
Look for the sculptors at work, carving statues that seem to be of Meresankh herself.
East wall of the first room: her father, Prince Kawab.
fun_fact: Her body waited 272 days for burial, and the dates were written on the doorway, a rare exact record of how long an Old Kingdom funeral took.
narration: You are inside the tomb of Queen Meresankh, and almost nowhere else at Giza keeps its colours like this. She had royal blood on every side. Her mother was a daughter of Khufu, her father was Khufu's eldest son, and she married King Khafre. She died at about 50, a small woman barely 1.54 metres tall. Her mother seems to have outlived her and prepared this tomb for her, and an inscription says she gave her daughter the black granite sarcophagus. Another inscription records that Meresankh was buried 272 days after she died, a long wait that may mean her death came suddenly. The archaeologist George Reisner found the tomb in 1927, on what was meant to be the last day of the dig. Robbers had been there first and thrown her skeleton into a corner. Look around the walls for her world: bakers, brewers, herdsmen, and sculptors carving her statues. Then find the row of ten women cut from the rock on the north side, probably Meresankh, her mother and her daughters, standing together for 4,500 years.

period: Old Kingdom, Fourth to Sixth Dynasty, c. 2580-2200 BC
summary: Khufu laid out his officials' tombs on a grid like a town: streets and blocks of the dead west of the Great Pyramid.
look: West of the Great Pyramid lies a sea of low, flat-topped rectangular tombs in rows, cut by straight 'streets'. The big early ones belonged to Khufu's relatives and officials, and G4000, Hemiunu's, is the largest of its group; later, smaller tombs squeeze into every gap. Most chapels are locked, and a few are opened in rotation.
story:
Mastaba is the Arabic word for a bench, and that is what these tombs look like. Above ground stood a solid block with a chapel and a false door, the carved stone doorway through which the dead person's spirit came to collect offerings. Behind a wall, a sealed room called the serdab held a statue. A shaft dropped through the block into the rock to the burial chamber.

Khufu planned this cemetery the way he planned his pyramid. The earliest tombs, in groups such as G2100 and G4000, stood in neat rows and held two oddities of his reign: slab stelae showing the owner at his offering table, and 'reserve heads', limestone portrait heads placed in the burial chambers. Nobody is sure why.

The digging was divided up with style. In 1902, at the Mena House Hotel, Italian, German and American teams agreed to share Giza, and Mary Reisner drew lots for three strips of this field. The Italians left in 1905, preferring sites with papyri. George Reisner's Harvard-Boston expedition worked here until 1947, and Hermann Junker's Austrian and German team dug the neighbouring cemeteries. Their records, plans and photographs are now online in the Giza Archives.
details: Walk down an east-west 'street': the big early tombs line up like houses in a planned suburb.
In any open chapel, the west wall: the false door, with the owner seated at his offering table.
The big block near the pyramid: G4000, the tomb of Hemiunu, probably the Great Pyramid's builder.
Seneb the dwarf, whose painted family statue is in Cairo, was buried in this field, in Junker's western cemetery.
If a guard offers to unlock a decorated chapel, a small tip is normal and usually worth it.
fun_fact: The Italians gave up their share of this cemetery in 1905 because they hoped to find papyri elsewhere. The Americans happily took it.
narration: You are looking at a town for the dead. West of the Great Pyramid, Khufu laid out the tombs of his officials in straight rows, with streets between them, like a planned suburb. Each one is a mastaba, the Arabic word for bench, because that is what they look like: a solid rectangular block of stone. Inside or against the block was a small chapel with a false door, a carved stone doorway through which the spirit of the dead came to collect offerings. Behind a wall, a sealed room held a statue, and a shaft dropped down through the rock to the burial chamber. The oldest and biggest tombs belonged to Khufu's relatives and top officials, and later generations squeezed smaller tombs into every gap. In 1902, at the Mena House Hotel, Italian, German and American archaeologists divided Giza between them, and Mary Reisner drew lots for strips of this field. Her husband George's team dug here for decades. Now look for the largest block near the pyramid: that is the tomb of Hemiunu, the man who probably built it.

period: Old Kingdom, Fourth Dynasty, reign of Khufu, c. 2570 BC
summary: Khufu's nephew and vizier, overseer of all the king's works, probably the man who built the Great Pyramid, and portrayed as proudly fat.
look: His tomb, mastaba G4000, is the large, battered stone block in the Western Cemetery just west of the Great Pyramid, noticeably bigger than its neighbours. There is nothing of him to see inside: his famous seated statue is in Hildesheim, Germany. Picture him instead, heavy and fleshy, sitting in a block-like stone seat.
story:
Hemiunu was family. His father was Prince Nefermaat, Khufu's elder brother, and his mother was Itet; their tomb at Meidum gave us the painted Meidum Geese. His grandfather was King Sneferu, the great pyramid builder of Dahshur. Hemiunu became vizier, the highest office below the king, keeper of the royal seal and, by royal decree, overseer of all the king's works. Most Egyptologists believe that made him the architect of the Great Pyramid, though no text says so outright.

In practice that meant surveying the site, running quarries and boats, and feeding thousands of workers, all without pulleys or iron tools.

His mastaba is the largest in its part of the field, and some of its blocks carry dates from Khufu's reign. In March 1912 Hermann Junker opened its walled-up statue room and found his seated statue. Robbers had been there first: they cut a child-sized hole in the wall, gouged out the inlaid eyes, broke the right arm and severed the head. The head was later restored, using a relief of Hemiunu to model the nose. The statue, now in the Roemer- und Pelizaeus-Museum in Hildesheim, is startlingly honest: a powerful man with rolls of fat on his chest, at a time when kings were shown lean and perfect.
details: Mastaba G4000: the large block just west of the Great Pyramid, bigger than every neighbour.
Compare its size with the rows of mastabas behind it: rank was measured in stone.
In Cairo, the Meidum Geese came from the chapel of his mother, Itet: same family.
If you look up his statue online, note the empty eye sockets where robbers dug out the inlays.
fun_fact: The robbers who looted his statue room got in through a hole just big enough for a child. What they wanted were the statue's inlaid eyes.
narration: Somewhere in this sea of tombs, just west of the Great Pyramid, lies the mastaba of the man who most likely built it. Hemiunu was family. His father was Khufu's elder brother, his grandfather was King Sneferu, and his mother's tomb chapel at Meidum gave us the famous painted geese. Under Khufu he became vizier, keeper of the royal seal and overseer of all the king's works. No inscription says in so many words that he designed the pyramid, but most Egyptologists believe he ran the project: the surveying, the quarries, the boats, the crews and their bread. In 1912 the archaeologist Hermann Junker opened his sealed statue room and found that robbers had got there first, through a hole just big enough for a child. They had gouged out the statue's inlaid eyes and knocked off its head. The restored statue is now in Hildesheim, in Germany, and it is startlingly honest: Hemiunu sits there heavy and fleshy, with rolls of fat on his chest. Look for the biggest block in these rows, and picture him sitting in it.

period: Old Kingdom, early Sixth Dynasty, c. 2340 BC
summary: A courtier's tomb you can often walk into: a columned porch, two seated statues and the classic Old Kingdom chapel.
look: In the cemetery south of the Great Pyramid and of the line of Khufu's causeway, on the way down towards the Sphinx, a columned porch opens in the face of a mastaba. Two seated statues of the owner flank the doorway, and inside are chapel rooms with false doors and offering scenes. Opening varies, but it is often accessible.
story:
Seshemnefer IV, numbered fourth among several officials of that name at Giza, was a courtier of the early Sixth Dynasty, around 2340 BC. He was head of the palace quarters where the royal women and children lived, and bore titles such as sole companion and secretary of secret royal commands.

Karl Lepsius's Prussian expedition explored the tomb in 1842-45 and took relief blocks to Berlin. Hermann Junker cleared it completely in the late 1920s, and five more reliefs went to Hildesheim: a grain harvest with donkeys carrying sacks to the granary, playing goats, bird-netting, a steer being slaughtered, and priests burning incense before Seshemnefer's statue. What stays here is the architecture.
details: The forecourt: two seated statues of Seshemnefer flank the entrance; their upper parts are restored.
The portico: columns carrying the roof of the porch, a fine survival on a private tomb.
Inside: the false doors, where priests laid bread, beer and incense for his spirit.
fun_fact: Pieces of the same tomb walls are now in two German cities: Lepsius took some to Berlin in the 1840s, and Junker's share went to Hildesheim.
narration: This small tomb with a columned porch belonged to Seshemnefer, the fourth official of that name buried at Giza, a courtier of the early Sixth Dynasty, about 2340 BC. He ran the palace quarters of the royal women and children and called himself sole companion of the king. It is a perfect pocket example of an Old Kingdom tomb: a forecourt, a portico, and a chapel with false doors where priests left bread, beer and incense for his spirit. The Prussian expedition of Karl Lepsius cut out reliefs for Berlin in the 1840s, and more went to Hildesheim after Hermann Junker cleared the tomb in the late 1920s. Look at the two seated statues of Seshemnefer guarding the entrance.

period: Old Kingdom, Fourth Dynasty, reign of Khafre, c. 2558-2532 BC
summary: It looks taller than the Great Pyramid but isn't: Khafre built on rock about 10 m higher, at a steeper angle, and kept his cap of casing.
look: The middle pyramid is about 136.4 m high today, with a cap of original smooth limestone casing on its top third. Its sides are about 215 m long and rise at about 53 degrees, steeper than Khufu's. Both entrances are on the north face, and at the north-west corner you can see where the bedrock was cut away in steps to make a level platform.
story:
Khafre was Khufu's son, and his pyramid was called 'Great is Khafre'. It was 143.5 m high originally, about 3 m less than his father's, with less volume, but it stands on bedrock some 10 m higher and its steeper slope makes it look the bigger of the two from most angles. The builders cut the north-west corner 10 m down into the rock and built up the south-east corner where the plateau slopes. The lowest course of casing was pink granite, the rest fine Tura limestone, which survives on the top third: the only Giza pyramid that still shows you its skin.

There are two entrances, one in the north face 11.5 m up and one at ground level, both leading to a burial chamber cut into the rock and roofed with gabled limestone beams. On 2 March 1818 Giovanni Belzoni, a giant from Padua who had once worked as a strongman in London, found the way in. The chamber was empty except for an open granite sarcophagus sunk into the floor, its lid broken, with animal bones he took to be a bull's. Robbers had long been there: an Arabic graffito probably dates from an opening recorded in 1372. Belzoni painted his own name and the date in large letters on the wall.

In the 1960s the physicist Luis Alvarez scanned the pyramid with cosmic-ray muons, the idea that found Khufu's Big Void in 2017. In the part he surveyed, he found no hidden rooms.
details: Top third: the surviving Tura limestone casing, the only original 'skin' left on a Giza pyramid.
North-west corner, at the base: bedrock cut into steps to level the site.
North face: two entrances, one about 11.5 m up and one at ground level.
Inside, on the burial chamber wall: Belzoni's painted 'Scoperta da G. Belzoni', with the date in March 1818.
East side: the ruins of the mortuary temple, and the causeway running down to the valley temple.
fun_fact: Belzoni's graffito begins 'Scoperta', Italian for 'discovered'. Explorers of his day signed monuments as freely as tourists carve benches.
narration: The middle pyramid belongs to Khufu's son Khafre, who ruled roughly 2558 to 2532 BC, and it is a beautiful optical trick. It looks taller than the Great Pyramid, but it is not. It was built on rock about 10 metres higher, and its sides rise more steeply, so from most angles it seems to win. Originally it stood 143.5 metres high, about 3 metres lower than his father's. Look up at the top third. That smooth pale surface is the original casing of fine Tura limestone, the only place at Giza where a pyramid still shows you its skin. Imagine the whole thing like that, white and polished, with a band of pink granite at the bottom. On the 2nd of March 1818 Giovanni Belzoni, a giant Italian who had worked as a strongman in London, found the way in. He reached a burial chamber cut into the rock and found it empty, except for an open granite sarcophagus sunk into the floor, with a few bones he thought belonged to a bull. Robbers had come centuries before. Belzoni painted his name and the date on the chamber wall in large letters, and if you go inside, you can still read it. Out here, look at the north-west corner, where the builders cut the bedrock away in steps, and then find the two entrances on the north face, one high up and one at ground level.

period: Old Kingdom, Fourth Dynasty, reign of Khafre, c. 2550 BC
summary: Old Kingdom architecture at its purest: red granite pillars, an alabaster floor and the empty places of 23 royal statues.
look: Beside the Sphinx stands a square, massive building of huge limestone blocks, faced with red Aswan granite. Inside, a T-shaped hall of square granite pillars, each a single block, carries granite beams over a floor of white Egyptian alabaster. There are no inscriptions or reliefs: just stone, and the marks in the floor where statues stood.
story:
This is the best-preserved temple of the Old Kingdom, and the way most visitors reach the Sphinx. Its core is limestone, some blocks weighing over 100 tonnes, faced with red granite brought down the Nile from Aswan. Two doors in the east face lead through a vestibule into the T-shaped hall. Its alabaster floor still shows the sockets where 23 statues of Khafre once stood, pale against the red granite in the dim light.

Most were plundered or smashed long ago. But around 1860 Auguste Mariette, clearing the sand here, found a pit containing a superb seated statue of Khafre, carved in a dark speckled stone usually called diorite, with the falcon god Horus spreading his wings behind the king's head. It is one of the masterpieces of Egyptian art, now in Cairo.

What happened here? Valley temples stood where the floodplain met the desert, so that boats could arrive. One theory is that the king's body was purified, or even embalmed, here before burial; another is that the temple served mainly for rituals for the statues. Neither is proven.

The interior granite is remarkably fresh, while the exterior limestone is deeply weathered. From the hall a passage leads to the causeway, which climbs nearly 500 m to the mortuary temple at the foot of the pyramid. Next door, the Sphinx lies in its quarry, and the unfinished Sphinx Temple sits right beside this one.
details: The T-shaped hall: square pillars, each cut from a single block of red granite, carrying granite beams.
The alabaster floor: rectangular marks where 23 statues of Khafre once stood.
Corners of the granite facing: some blocks are cut in an L shape to wrap around a corner in one piece.
Outside: compare the weathered limestone core with the crisp granite inside.
Follow the passage out to the causeway and the terrace beside the Sphinx.
fun_fact: The dark stone of Khafre's statues came from a desert quarry in Nubia, not far from Abu Simbel, which you will see on the 17th.
narration: You are inside the best-preserved temple of the Old Kingdom, built for Khafre about 4,500 years ago. Notice what is missing: there are no carvings, no paintings, no texts. The power is all in the stone. The walls are a limestone core, with some blocks weighing over 100 tonnes, faced with red granite shipped down the Nile from Aswan. The square pillars of this T-shaped hall are each a single block of granite, and the floor is white Egyptian alabaster. Look down at the floor and you can still see the marks where 23 statues of the king once stood, glowing pale against the red granite in the dim light. Almost all were carried away or smashed. But around 1860 Auguste Mariette, clearing the sand from this temple, found a pit containing one that survived: Khafre enthroned, carved in a dark speckled stone, with the falcon god Horus spreading his wings behind the king's head. It is one of the great masterpieces in Cairo. Why build such a place? Valley temples stood where the floodplain met the desert, so the king's funeral could arrive by boat. Some think his body was purified or embalmed here, others that the temple was mainly for rituals for the statues. From here a causeway nearly 500 metres long climbed to the pyramid. Before you leave the hall, find a corner where a granite block bends around it in one piece.

period: Old Kingdom, Fourth Dynasty, reign of Khafre, c. 2550 BC
summary: A ruin, but an important one: the first pyramid temple with the full five-part plan that later kings copied.
look: Against the east face of Khafre's pyramid lie the stumps of a large temple built of colossal limestone blocks. From its front, the line of the causeway runs east and down the slope towards the Sphinx and the valley temple.
story: Ruined as it is, this temple set the standard. It is the first to have all five elements of later pyramid temples: an entrance hall, an open court with pillars, five niches for statues of the king, five storerooms, and an inner sanctuary against the pyramid. More than 50 life-size statues of Khafre once stood here; they were removed and recycled, possibly under Ramesses II. Its blocks are colossal, the largest estimated at around 400 tonnes. The covered causeway, 494.6 m long, linked it to the valley temple. Even a door lintel had a second life: the Dream Stele between the Sphinx's paws is a granite lintel reused from this temple.
details: The biggest limestone blocks in the walls: among the heaviest stones ever moved at Giza.
Try to trace the open court, the heart of the plan, among the fallen blocks.
Turn east and follow the causeway with your eyes, down to the valley temple beside the Sphinx.
fun_fact: The stone between the Sphinx's paws, Thutmose IV's Dream Stele, began life as a door lintel here, more than a thousand years before he reused it.
narration: These ruins against the east face of Khafre's pyramid were his mortuary temple, where priests brought offerings to the king every day. It looks like a field of giant stones, but it matters: this is the first temple with the full plan every later pyramid temple copied. An entrance hall, an open court with pillars, five niches for statues of the king, five storerooms, and a sanctuary against the pyramid. More than 50 life size statues of Khafre once stood here. Some blocks weigh hundreds of tonnes. Even a door lintel had a second life: it is now the Dream Stele between the Sphinx's paws. Now turn east and follow the line of the causeway, almost 500 metres long, down to the valley temple.

period: Old Kingdom, Fourth Dynasty, reign of Menkaure, c. 2500 BC
summary: The smallest of the three, with a skirt of Aswan granite and a great gash torn by a sultan who spent eight months trying to demolish it.
look: The third pyramid is about 61 m high now, originally about 65 m, with a base of a little over 100 m: roughly a tenth of the Great Pyramid's volume. Around the bottom you can still see red Aswan granite casing, mostly left rough and smoothed only around the entrance on the north face. Above that entrance, the north face is torn open by a vertical gash.
story:
Menkaure was Khafre's son, and his pyramid was called 'Menkaure is Divine'. It is small but lavish: the lowest 16 courses were to be cased in red granite from Aswan, with white limestone above. The king died before the work was done. Much of the granite was never smoothed, and his successor Shepseskaf finished the temples hastily in mud-brick.

In 1196 Saladin's son, the sultan al-Aziz Uthman, decided to demolish the pyramids and started with this one. His workers spent eight months on it, pulling loose one or two stones a day with wedges, levers and ropes. Then he gave up, leaving the great scar on the north face.

In 1837 Colonel Howard Vyse found the entrance and, in a granite-lined burial chamber, a basalt sarcophagus carved like a palace facade. He shipped it to England on the Beatrice, which sank in a storm in 1838. He also found the lid of a wooden coffin naming Menkaure, now in the British Museum, but radiocarbon dates it to around 1000 BC: a restoration by priests long after the king's burial.

The valley temple below gave George Reisner a famous prize: slate triads of Menkaure with the goddess Hathor and a province goddess, and a pair statue of the king with his queen. The Greeks had their own story. Some said this pyramid was built by a courtesan called Rhodopis, or Doricha, the lover of Sappho's brother Charaxos. Herodotus dismissed the tale.
details: North face, low down: the entrance, with the granite around it smoothed while elsewhere it was left rough.
Above the entrance: the great vertical gash left by al-Aziz Uthman's demolition attempt of 1196.
Around the base: fallen and unfinished granite blocks, some still with their rough outer surface.
East face: the low remains of the mortuary temple, finished in mud-brick by Shepseskaf.
South side: Menkaure's three small queens' pyramids in a row.
fun_fact: In 2024 a plan to put the fallen granite blocks back on the pyramid was announced, then dropped within weeks after archaeologists objected.
narration: The third and smallest pyramid belonged to Menkaure, Khafre's son and Khufu's grandson, about 2500 BC. It has only a tenth of the Great Pyramid's volume, but it was dressed in the most expensive stone. The lowest 16 courses were to be cased in red granite from Aswan, more than 900 kilometres up the Nile. Menkaure died before it was finished. Look at the bottom courses: most of the granite was never smoothed, and only around the entrance on the north face was it dressed flat. Now look above the entrance at the huge vertical scar. In 1196 Saladin's son, the sultan al-Aziz Uthman, decided to demolish the pyramids and started with this one. His men worked for eight months, pulling down one or two stones a day, and then he gave up. In 1837 Colonel Howard Vyse broke into the burial chamber and found a basalt sarcophagus carved like a palace. He shipped it to England on a boat called the Beatrice, which sank in a storm in 1838, so Menkaure's sarcophagus now lies at the bottom of the sea. The Greeks told a different story about this pyramid: that it was built by a courtesan called Rhodopis, or Doricha, the lover of the poet Sappho's brother. Herodotus did not believe it. Before you move on, find the place where the smooth granite around the entrance meets the rough, unfinished blocks.
